USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: The US should engage China in negotiations without committing to new escalatory actions. The tariff war has now reached a point where continued escalation carries material domestic economic risk. The upcoming Sept 1 List 4A implementation should proceed as already announced (credibility), but no new tariff threats should be added. Signal willingness to talk seriously about enforcement mechanisms and structural issues while holding the current line.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.35 reflects that the trade war is now inflicting measurable damage on the US economy, though not yet existential. Key evidence: (1) US manufacturing PMI fell to 49.9 in August — first contraction in nearly a decade (IHS Markit, Aug 22), with new orders dropping the most in 10 years and export sales at their lowest since 2009. (2) Gross private domestic investment tumbled 5.5% in Q2, the worst since Q4 2015, pulling a full percentage point from GDP growth (CNBC, Aug 26). (3) The yield curve inverted further — 3-month T-bills yielding 32bp above 10-year notes — a reliable recession predictor (Axios, Aug 6). (4) Morgan Stanley warns global recession within 6-9 months if tariffs go to 25% across the board (CNBC, Aug 26). (5) CBO estimates tariffs will reduce real US GDP by 0.3% by 2020 (Fox Business, Aug 21). (6) Farm belt support eroding — farmer approval of Trump dropped from 79% to 71% in one month (Farm Journal, Aug 23); farm bankruptcies up 13% (NBC, Aug 11); China halted all US agricultural purchases (CNBC, Aug 10). (7) The Fed itself reported tariffs have had 'material' impact on manufacturing growth (Globe and Mail, Jul 5).

However, the threat is not existential for the US because: (a) The Fed's own model estimates implemented tariffs reduce US GDP by only 0.19% long-run (Federal Reserve FEDS Notes, Jul 15), and even full escalation only 0.31% — modest. (b) China faces worse structural damage — their GDP impact is comparable but they also face capital flight risk from yuan depreciation, $3T in external debt, and food inflation at 7% (LA Times, Aug 13). (c) The US has stronger negotiating leverage: China's economy is slowing faster, the yuan has broken 7 for the first time since 2008 (NPR, Aug 11), and China is burning political capital defending its currency.

The action score of -0.15 (mild negotiate) reflects that the US should hold firm on existing tariffs but not add new ones. Escalation would be counterproductive given manufacturing is already contracting and recession fears are real. But concession is premature — China has not offered structural reforms on IP, tech transfer, or enforcement. The rational move is to keep the pressure that exists (the $250B at 25% and upcoming List 4A) while creating space for talks to address the structural issues that tariffs alone cannot solve. The split of List 4 into 4A (Sept 1) and 4B (Dec 15) already provides a natural de-escalation lever — delay or modify 4B if talks show genuine progress.
key_factors: US manufacturing PMI contraction (49.9, first in decade)
Yield curve inversion deepening — recession signal
Farm belt political pressure rising — China halted ag purchases
GDP growth slowing to ~1.5% annualized per PMI data
CBO: tariffs reducing US GDP by 0.3% by 2020
China under greater structural stress (yuan past 7, capital flight risk, $3T external debt)
No structural reform offers from China yet — premature to concede

sources_cited.excerpt: The U.S. manufacturing PMI was 49.9 in August, below the neutral 50.0 threshold for the first time since September 2009. New orders received by manufacturers dropped the most in 10 years, while export sales tanked to the lowest level since August 2009.

Morgan Stanley says that the global economy would fall into recession if the U.S. raises tariffs on all imports from China to 25% and Beijing follows suit. Gross private domestic investment tumbled 5.5% in the second quarter, the worst since the fourth quarter of 2015.
CBO expects the changes in U.S. and foreign trade policies since January 2018 to reduce the level of real U.S. GDP by about 0.3 percent by 2020.

China announces retaliation on ~$75B of US goods (5-10%, split Sept 1 / Dec 15), including re-imposing tariffs on US autos. Trump orders US companies to 'immediately start looking for an alternative to China.'
After CNY breaks 7 per USD, US Treasury designates China a currency manipulator (first such designation since 1994).
China let the yuan drop to its lowest value since 2008. The currency is now trading at just over 7 yuan to the dollar. The U.S. Treasury Department labeled China a 'currency manipulator.'
Farm Journal found 71 percent of farmers approve of what Trump is doing, down from 79 percent in July. Soybean prices dropped from $5.70 to $3.96 per bushel locally.
The direct long-run impact of the currently implemented tariffs on Chinese output is likely to be small, effectively reducing the level of real GDP by 0.25 percent. US GDP would fall by 0.19 percent.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain current retaliatory posture without further escalation. Signal willingness to resume talks in September while holding firm on core positions (Huawei delisting, tariff rollback as precondition). Do not concede on structural reform demands, but do not provoke additional US escalation either. The situation is too economically damaging to escalate further and too politically charged to concede.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is severe and accelerating. The tariff coverage now extends to nearly all Chinese exports to the US — List 3 at 25% on $250B, List 4A at 15% from Sept 1, List 4B at 15% from Dec 15 — representing an unprecedented assault on China's export-driven growth model. China's economy is already showing material damage: industrial production growth collapsed to 4.8% in July (17-year low, well below the 5.8% consensus), GDP slowed to 6.2% in Q2 (27-year low), retail sales missed expectations at 7.6% vs 8.6% forecast, and urban unemployment rose to 5.3%. The industry ministry itself acknowledged 'arduous efforts' are needed to meet 2019 targets (Reuters, July 23). Supply chains are actively relocating out of China, with manufacturers moving capacity to neighboring countries (Reuters, July 23). The Huawei entity list — expanded to 115 affiliates by August 21 — threatens China's tech champion and its 5G ambitions, cutting off access to critical US semiconductor and software inputs. The currency manipulator designation (August 5) adds a new dimension of pressure, even as the IMF confirmed China's yuan is 'broadly in line with fundamentals' and reserves remain adequate at ~$3.2T.

However, China retains meaningful leverage. Its retaliatory tariffs on $75B of US goods (announced August 23) target politically sensitive US sectors — soybeans, crude oil, autos, pork — hitting US farm belt constituencies ahead of the 2020 election cycle. The rare earth supply chain card (signaled by Xi's Jiangxi visit on May 20) remains unplayed. The 'unreliable entity list' announced May 31 provides a retaliatory framework. And the US faces its own costs: the Fed signaled willingness to cut rates amid trade uncertainty, and Trump's 'order' for US companies to leave China (August 23) was widely viewed as impractical and alarming to business.

The action stance is cautious (-0.1) because further escalation is asymmetrically dangerous for China. With nearly all US imports from China already tariffed, China's remaining retaliatory capacity is limited. Meanwhile, the US can still expand coverage and raise rates further (Trump has threatened 30% on Lists 1-3). The September negotiation window — referenced by Kudlow as recently as August 22 — offers the only viable off-ramp. Conceding now on structural demands (IP transfer, industrial subsidies, Made in China 2025) would be politically impossible domestically and would undermine CCP legitimacy. But matching Trump's escalations tit-for-tat risks a spiral that China's slowing economy cannot absorb. The optimal play is to hold the line, signal willingness to talk, and let US domestic political costs (farm distress, business uncertainty, market volatility) create pressure for a more balanced negotiation.
key_factors: Industrial production at 17-year low (4.8% in July), GDP at 27-year low (6.2% Q2) — trade war is materially damaging China's economy
Huawei entity list expanded to 115 affiliates, threatening China's 5G and semiconductor ambitions
Near-complete tariff coverage: List 3 (25%, $250B) + List 4A (15%, Sept 1) + List 4B (15%, Dec 15) covers virtually all Chinese exports to US
China's retaliatory capacity is limited — already targeting $75B of US goods, running out of US imports to tariff
Currency manipulator designation adds financial pressure despite IMF contradicting the label
Supply chain relocation accelerating as manufacturers move capacity out of China
September negotiation window offers potential off-ramp; US domestic costs (farm belt, business uncertainty) creating countervailing pressure

sources_cited.excerpt: After the Shanghai round, Trump announces 10% tariffs on the remaining ~$300B of Chinese goods (List 4), effective Sept 1.
After CNY breaks 7 per USD, US Treasury designates China a currency manipulator (first such designation since 1994).

China announces retaliation on ~$75B of US goods (5-10%, split Sept 1 / Dec 15), including re-imposing tariffs on US autos. Trump orders US companies to 'immediately start looking for an alternative to China' and directs a 5-point increase on the planned List 4 rate (to 15%) and threatened hikes on existing lists.

Industrial production in China grew just 4.8% in July compared to a year earlier. That's the worst growth for that sector in 17 years. Other important measures: retail sales grew 7.6% vs expected 8.6%. Urban unemployment increased to 5.3% from 5.1% in June.

China's economic growth slowed to 6.2% in the second quarter, its weakest pace in at least 27 years. The prolonged trade war is pushing some Chinese and foreign manufacturers to move capacity to neighbouring countries and rebuild supply chains outside of China.
This rule adds 46 additional non-US affiliates of Huawei to the Entity List, raising total Huawei-affected entities to 115.

IMF concluded that the exchange rate of the Chinese yuan was 'broadly in line with medium-term fundamentals' and that PBOC had 'little FX intervention'. At about US$3.2 trillion, China's foreign currency reserves remain more than adequate.
